title: How the Mainstream Recruits for the Manosphere
author: Aaron Renn
summary: Aaron Renn argues that mainstream voices push young men toward the manosphere by condemning male influencers rather than understanding their appeal. He examines three examples: a survey finding that two-thirds of young Democratic women think women's problems are largely caused by men, a viral X thread giving young men an eleven-step plan to attract women, and a Leonard Sax op-ed urging men to be gentlemen. Each, he says, displays one-sided blame, instrumental treatment of men, or selective revival of old norms without the social ecosystem that supported them. He offers four principles for talking to young men: ground rhetoric in statistical reality, acknowledge that women have faults too, avoid retro appeals divorced from context, and deliver tough messages with empathy and skin in the game, as Jordan Peterson did.
points: Mainstream commentators tend to condemn manosphere figures rather than ask why young men are drawn to them, which cedes the audience.
One signature appeal of the manosphere is stating true statistics that mainstream discussion rarely mentions.
Lectures that put all the onus on men, such as the viral eleven-step dating thread, read as instrumental and are easily debunked online.
Calling men to be gentlemen without the broader social ecosystem that gave the idea meaning is the 'trad con' approach and does not persuade.
Effective messages to young men need statistical honesty, balance about women's faults, no selective retro norms, and real empathy and skin in the game.
quotes: But they’ve seldom tried to understand why young men are attracted to those figures. They prefer to condemn rather than figure out how to compete.

There’s an old saying that unless you meet someone where they are, you have no moral authority to lead them anywhere else.
Fourth, delivering tough messages to men requires empathy and skin in their game.
